newsitem.title: PERU: Peruvian guerrillas plan next move - spokesman.
newsitem.headline: Peruvian guerrillas plan next move - spokesman.

text.p: Marxist guerrilla strategists are meeting at a secret location in Peru to plan their next move in the 9-day-old siege of the Japanese ambassador's residence, their self-styled international spokesman said on Thursday.
"The last news that I have is that the national committee is meeting now to decide upon the next steps," Isaac Velazco told Reuters by telephone from Hamburg, Germany.

Velazco, who said he was granted political asylum in Germany in 1994 after fleeing Peru in November 1993, said the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) had successfully achieved its first aim of drawing world attention to its motives and beliefs and was now concentrating on how to obtain the freedom of its militants behind bars in Peru.

"The first stage, which we called 'Breaking the Silence,' has been fulfilled," he said. "Thanks to the successful takeover of the residence the entire world is today talking about the brutality of the regime of (President Alberto) Fujimori, of the political repression in Peru and the impunity of the armed forces."

A 20-person MRTA commando unit stormed the residence on Dec. 17 and was still holding 103 VIP hostages on Thursday after releasing at various times nearly 400 others who were captured during a lavish reception.
Velazco said the rebels would stay in the embassy for as long as it took to achieve their aim of freeing jailed comrades.

"We will be waiting. The Peruvian people have suffered 500 years of exploitation so we have all the time in the world," he said. He accused Fujimori of heading a government responsible for "policies of terrorism against the people" and said the government's refusal to negotiate with the MRTA showed "intransigency and arrogance."

"It is the government that is denying a dialogue. They are provoking a bloody, military solution," Velazco said. "We are a political movement and all political movements use dialogue. We are prepared to look for halfway points to discuss."

Fujimori has flatly refused a rebel demand for the release of prisoners. In his only public words during the crisis, he said he would guarantee that force would not be used only if the guerrillas surrendered their weapons and freed their captives.

Velazco said the rebels continued to propose the release of their comrades from jail, followed by the transportation by plane of fighters inside the residence to a safe jungle zone. "Of course they cannot go alone. They would have to be sent with guarantors, some of the hostages," he said.

Velazco dismissed the idea that the government might offer the rebels political exile in Cuba as "pure speculation." He declined to confirm information from the anti-terrorism police that another MRTA unit was in Lima waiting to strike in case the government tried to storm the besieged residence.
"Clearly, we are not going to announce our plans in advance. But obviously the MRTA has a structure of support units ready throughout the country," he said.
Velazco said the MRTA had not repeated its earlier threats to kill hostages because it was concentrating on working for a negotiated solution without harm to the hostages.

"At all times, the hostages have been treated with the utmost respect, dignity and humanity," he said. "However, neither this nor the previous releases of hostages should be interpreted as weakness, as the government propagandists would like. That is a lamentable mistake."
